title: Chapter 15: The Cable Comes Down
content: The torch is lit at 7:12 and Wren can see the flame from her kitchen window, a small blue star with a white heart in it, and she puts her cup down and goes out without her coat.
By the time she is down the lane there are four men on the east ramp and a flatbed truck backed to the tower and a spool the size of a hay bale sitting on it, empty, waiting.

The foreman is called Coates and he is from Parkersburg and he has the county's removal order in a plastic sleeve, taped to the leg of the tower where anybody can read it. He sees her coming and he does the thing they all do, which is to look at her boots first.
"Ma'am. We are going to need the ramp."
"It is a public landing."
"It is a condemned landing as of Tuesday." He says it without relish. "I have got a signed order and a crane coming at nine."
"Then you have got two hours."
"I have got an order."
Wren looks at the boat. It is tied at the east ramp with the apron down and the wheelhouse door open the way she left it, and the fog is on the water so thick that the far bank is a rumour.
"Two hours," she says. "The crane can wait at the top of the lane."
Coates thinks about it, and looks at the four men, and looks at her, and something in his face does the arithmetic that men his age do when they have been in a town for one morning.
"Two hours," he says. "Do not make me regret it."

The order says what orders say. Condemnation of a crossing structure, Mile 9, Sable River. Removal of cable, drum, and appurtenances. Restoration of the bank to the condition described in Exhibit C. Authorized by the District Engineer, District 4, Basin Authority, and below that a signature she has seen on a survey, on a routing slip, on a form he brought to her house in the dark.
T. Marsh, PE.
Ade comes down the lane at 7:30 with his hands in his pockets and stands beside her without saying anything, which is the way he has stood beside her since September.
"You knew," he says.
"I knew Tuesday."
"Four minutes."
"Four minutes." She watches the men unroll the hose. "I got to thirty-eight names."
"Out of forty."
"Thirty-eight. And then the chairman put his hand up, and I said the last two anyway, and the transcript says unintelligible, which is a word they use for a woman finishing a sentence."
Ade is quiet. Then he says, "Who were the last two?"
"Elias Aubrey and Ade Kessler."
He looks at her.
"You are not dead," she says. "It was the only way I could get your name into a county document."
Ade laughs, one short breath of it, and then stops, because the torch has gone from blue to white and the sound has started.

The cable comes out of the water at the tower and goes up over the sheave and down into the drum house, and it is an inch and three eighths of galvanized steel, seven hundred and forty feet of it, laid in 1974 and re-swaged twice, and it is the only thing on this river that has held for fifty-two years without being asked.
The man in the leather apron puts the torch to it at the thimble, where the cable is served and wrapped and bolted into the eye, and the flame is not a flame, it is a sound with a light in it.

The steel goes red, then orange, then the colour of a thing that is no longer steel. Sparks come off it in a slow spray that lands on the wet gravel and dies there. The smell is hot iron and burnt grease and something under that which is the river burning off the cable.
It takes four minutes. Wren counts them, because counting is what she does.
At the fourth minute the torch comes away and the man in the apron steps back and says something to Coates that the wind takes.
The cable does not fall.

It hangs there for a second and a half, still holding, with a bead of molten steel at the cut and the whole weight of the river behind it, and Wren has time to think that this is what it must have looked like on the twelfth, the moment before, when the water was still at the second rung and the deck was still a deck.
Then it goes.

The cut end drops and hits the ramp with a crack that goes up through the planks and into her feet, and the drum, which has been holding seven hundred and forty feet of tension since before she was born, spins free with a shriek and pays out forty feet of cable into the water in one long iron snake, and the spray comes up over the apron, and the ferry rocks, and is still.
Nobody says anything. The men stand with their tools. Up on the bank a dog is barking at a house where nobody has come out.

The cable lies in the water now, all of it, from the east tower to the west, on the bottom where it has always been on the bottom between the towers, and the only difference is that there is nobody at either end of it.
Ade takes off his boots.
"Ade."
"It is going in the water," he says. "It has been in the water fifty years. It can go in the water with somebody holding it."

He wades in to his knees, then his thighs, then his waist, and the cold takes his breath out in a sound she can hear from the ramp. He gets his hand on the cut end before the current takes it under, and he pulls it up, and the water runs off it, and he walks it back up the gravel with the cable over his shoulder, hand over hand, forty feet of it, and he lays it down at the top of the ramp and stands there holding the end of it in both hands.
Coates looks at him. "Sir, that is county property."
Ade does not answer. He holds the end of the cable the way a man holds a rope at a funeral, which is not the way you hold a rope.

Wren stands at the top of the east ramp and does not move. She has not moved since the torch was lit. Somebody brings a folding chair and sets it behind her and says something about sitting down, and she says no thank you, and the chair stays there, empty, for the rest of the morning.

The crane comes at nine. The men run the cable onto the spool with a winch, and it comes up out of the water black and streaming and wrapped in weed, and the spool turns and turns and takes it, and the whole river bottom comes up with it in pieces: a bicycle frame, a bucket, a length of chain, a licence plate from a year she does not recognise.

Ruthie comes down at nine thirty with a box of coffee and a tray of cups and stands at the top of the bank, and does not hand anything out, because it is not that kind of morning. She sets the box on the tailgate of somebody's truck. Ida Quill is there. Tobe Quill is there, eleven, in a coat three sizes too big, standing with his hands in his pockets and his eyes on the water where the cable used to come up.
"Does it still work," Tobe says. "The boat."
"Not without the cable," Wren says.
"Then what is it."
"It is a boat."
He thinks about that the way he thought about the depth, five weeks ago, and he does not ask the next question, which is the one about what happens to a boat that is only a boat.

The ferry is towed off the east ramp at ten, and it is a strange thing to watch, because a cable ferry does not go anywhere sideways. They take it on a line from the west bank and it comes across the river broadside, dragging its apron, with the wheelhouse door still open and the drum turning slowly for no reason at all.
Before they take it, Wren goes aboard.

The log is already out, in the house, wrapped in a towel. The tide clock is not worth taking. Under the bench in the wheelhouse there is a tin of spare split pins, a codline, a handline, and the brass bell that Elias took off a sunken launch in 1983 and bolted to the frame, and she puts her hand on the bell and finds the two screws.
Coates is on the deck. "That is county property now."
"Then send me a form," she says.
He looks at her for a moment. Then he takes his screwdriver out of his back pocket and hands it to her, handle first, and looks away while she takes the bell off the frame.

The bell is heavier than it looks. She carries it down the apron and up the ramp and sets it on the gravel at the foot of the tower, and when she turns around the boat is already moving, and she can see the letters on the hull, AUBREY'S, in white paint that has been renewed every April since before she was born, and the plate welded at the bow that says nine.

She puts her hand flat on the plate as the boat goes past the end of the ramp, and then it is out of reach, and then it is across the river, and then it is on the flatbed and strapped down and gone up the lane at ten past eleven.
There is a wet line on the bank where the cable was dragged out. It will dry by afternoon.

The men put up the fence before they leave. Posts, wire, a gate, four hundred feet of it along the top of the bank and down both sides of the ramp, and it takes them forty minutes, and Wren stands and watches them do it because she is not going to leave the landing to strangers.
Then Coates comes over with the sign, which is corrugated plastic on two steel posts, and he has a drill, and he asks her, actually asks her, whether she wants to be the one to put it up.
"No," she says.
He puts it up.
MILE 9 CROSSING. CLOSED BY ORDER OF THE BASIN AUTHORITY. For inquiries write to: Basin Authority, District 4, Post Office Box 1180, Columbus, Ohio 43215.
No telephone. A post office box, two hundred and six miles away, in a city where nobody has ever seen this river.

The sign goes over the old one, which was wood, and which has been on that post since before the county put up signs. Coates drills it flat and steps back, and the wind gets under the corner of the new plastic, and the corner lifts, and under it, in white paint on a green board, there is a letter and three numbers.

Wren stands at the fence with her hand on the cold wire and reads the address in Columbus, and the corner of the plastic lifts and falls, lifts and falls, and she does not take her hand off the wire, and behind her the river goes on doing what it has done since before there was a county to write it down.
highlight: The county cuts the cable at 7:12 and fences the landing, and Wren reads 1908 under the new sign.
